<reason>B won because it kept the proposition as a choice of main instrument, paired essential-use protection with pricing of excess, and forced a cleaner decision rule: A would still prefer bans even if prices secured the needed savings. A was punchier on equity and timing, and B never fully erased the paid-lawn problem, but B answered pressure honestly, treated backstops as contingencies rather than a collapse of its case, and made the debate easier to decide on water-security grounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s closing use of A’s A1: even if steep prices met the savings target while protecting essentials, A would still ban paid lawns—converting A’s civic-equality claim into a concession that uniform prohibitions mattered more than securing supply.</best_rebuttal>
